newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia sets world's largest reclamation project.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sets world's largest reclamation project.

text.p: The world's tallest towers are ready for occupancy, the longest building is in planning and now Malaysia's latest candidate for the Guinness record book -- an international airport on the world's largest reclamation project -- has been given the green light.

The new airport would be built on a manmade island under a 30-billion ringgit ($12 billion) sea reclamation project off the coast of northern Kedah state, companies and officials associated with the project said.

Tourism facilities, petrochemical storage tanks and industrial parks for the aerospace and defence industries would be built on other islands, attracting a total investment of 80 billion ringgit over the 20-year life of the project's development, state officials said.

Marine Engineering firm Hock Seng Lee Bhd (HSL) said in a statement to the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange on Monday night it has been awarded "the sole turnkey project for the reclamation and associated engineering works".
Kedah Chief Minister Sanusi Junid said last week he had received approval for the project by fax from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who is on two-month leave abroad.
Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, said the project would go ahead pending an Environmental Impact Assessment.

"Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has given his views on the urgency for the implementation of the project," Anwar told reporters in Kuala Lumpur last week. HSL would build the first 2,800 hectares (6,900 acres) island to be the site of the new airport and seaport. A second island of 3,500 hectares (8,640 acres) would be an industrial zone.

The master plan calls for nine sausage-shaped islands to be created covering 16,300 hectares (40,277 acres). They would be built 500 metres (yards) to a kilometre (0.6 miles) offshore of Kedah, Mahathir's home state and one of Malaysia's least developed .

The state government last month named as the overall project developer Kuala Lumpur-based Samudera Baru Darul Aman Sdn Bhd, a company in which HSL executive chairman Dennis Yee Chee Ming has a 25 percent stake.
The major question mark over the project is who is going to come up with the money to finance it, analysts said.
"You are talking about a very long-term project," said Audrey Ho, head of research at Mohaiyani Securities. "The question is, who is going to fork out the money."

"Whoever is given the contracts will obviously make money, but whether the project will wind up as a white elephant nobody really can make that call today," she said. "But if you don't have infrastructure in place you can't attract investment."
The project may be floated on the stock market under rules allowing infrastructure projects to be listed, analysts said.

HSL, Malaysia's leading land reclamation company, stands to be a big winner. The company, based in Malaysia's Borneo state of Sarawak, debuted on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange last June at 7.80 ringgit and watched its share price rocket to a high of 54 ringgit earlier this year. It opened on Tuesday at 39 ringgit.
The Kedah reclamation project "will springboard HSL to a new dimension", Sarawak Securities Research said in note to clients last month.

It is the latest in a series of "mega-projects" in Malaysia that includes the 452-metre (1,483 feet) Petronas twin towers and a planned 1.8 km (1.1 mile) long building called Gigaworld to be built on stilts over Kuala Lumpur's Klang River.

Other projects include the $3.5 billion Kuala Lumpur International Airport, an $8 billion new federal capital, the $5.5 billion Bakun dam, and a multi-billion dollar zone for information technology companies.
